articles.title: Rochdale AFC Signs Goalkeeper Tasker on Loan from Premier League Club
articles.excerpt: Rochdale AFC has announced the signing of winger Glenn Middleton from Doncaster Rovers on a one-year deal, alongside a loan agreement for defender Charlie Tasker from Brighton.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale AFC has confirmed the signing of winger Glenn Middleton from Doncaster Rovers on a one-year contract. The announcement was made on 1 September 2026, marking a significant addition to the League Two side's squad ahead of the new season.

Glenn Middleton, 26, has a notable footballing background, having previously played for clubs including Rangers, where he made 29 appearances, and Dundee United. He joined Doncaster Rovers last summer on a free transfer, where he featured 35 times in League One. Head coach Ian Watson expressed enthusiasm about Middleton's arrival, highlighting his pace and experience as key attributes that will benefit the team.

In addition to Middleton, Rochdale has also secured a loan deal for young defender Charlie Tasker from Premier League side Brighton. Tasker has captained Brighton's under-21 side in the Premier League 2, adding depth to Rochdale's defensive options. Tasker is expected to provide valuable support to the team's backline as they prepare for the competitive season ahead.

The signings of Middleton and Tasker are expected to bolster Rochdale's squad as they prepare for the challenges of the upcoming season. Fans will be eager to see how these new additions impact the team's performance on the pitch.

articles.title: Tram Services Disrupted in Rochdale This Weekend Due to Maintenance Works
articles.excerpt: No trams will operate between Freehold and Rochdale Town Centre on Saturday, with further service changes on Sunday due to maintenance works.
articles.content_html:
This Saturday, 3 September, no tram services will operate between Freehold and Rochdale Town Centre. This disruption is part of ongoing maintenance and improvement works on the Metrolink network.

On Sunday, 4 September, from the start of service until 11am, additional works will take place at Deansgate-Castlefield and Trafford Bar, resulting in further service changes across the network. Travellers are advised to plan their journeys accordingly.

In addition, the lift at Derker tram stop is currently out of service, affecting step-free access. Passengers travelling towards Manchester can use a ramp from Cromford Street to access the Manchester-bound platform, while those heading towards Rochdale should use the same ramp and cross the tracks to reach the Rochdale-bound platform.

Passengers requiring step-free access at Heaton Park tram stop should note that the lifts are also out of service. They are encouraged to contact the Metrolink customer service centre at 0161 244 1000 for assistance with journey planning. Lines are open from 7am to 8pm on weekdays and 8am to 8pm on weekends and bank holidays.

articles.title: Planning Application for Roof Replacement at Middleton Care Provider Refused
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has refused planning permission for Vestacare's proposal to replace the roof and alter the appearance of its offices in Middleton, citing concerns over the design's compatibility with the surrounding area.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has refused planning permission for Vestacare's proposal to replace the roof and alter the appearance of its offices and distribution centre located at Unit 1 Westcroft Industrial Estate, 582 Manchester Old Road in Middleton. The council deemed the plans "out of character" with the surrounding area, which is primarily composed of various commercial and industrial buildings.

Vestacare, a care provider that supports adults with learning disabilities, submitted the application to replace the existing asbestos roof and external cladding, as well as to extend the shallow pitched roof over the entire building. In their design and access statement, the company argued that the proposal aimed to refurbish and modernise the existing industrial building, which they described as having fragmented and visually inconsistent roof forms.

The statement also highlighted that several adjacent units within the estate have undergone refurbishment, suggesting that their proposal was in line with the ongoing regeneration of the area. Vestacare indicated that the improved roof structure would enhance internal storage and distribution arrangements for their care home operations across the region.

Following the council's decision, Vestacare will need to consider alternative options for addressing the condition of the building's roof and cladding, while ensuring compliance with local planning regulations. The refusal of the application may impact their operational efficiency, as the current roof condition poses challenges for their distribution facility.

articles.title: Mountain Rescue Team Finds Missing 71-Year-Old Man Near Piethorne Reservoir
articles.excerpt: A 71-year-old man with dementia was found by a mountain rescue team near Piethorne Reservoir after being reported missing on Saturday. The search involved police and a helicopter.
articles.content_html:
A mountain rescue team successfully located a 71-year-old man with dementia who had been reported missing near Piethorne Reservoir in Newhey on Saturday evening. The search operation was initiated after Greater Manchester Police received a report regarding the missing individual, prompting a coordinated effort that included the use of a police helicopter.

The Oldham Mountain Rescue Team was called in to assist with the search. According to a statement from the team, the man was equipped with an air tag that indicated he was in the vicinity of the reservoir. Initial searches conducted by police and the helicopter did not yield any results, leading to the involvement of the mountain rescue team.

The rescue team mobilised to the dam wall at Piethorne Reservoir, where their water section began searching the edges of the water both on foot and using a raft. Meanwhile, two additional search sections covered paths and tracks that had not yet been searched by police. Search dogs were also deployed to aid in the effort.

The missing man was found by a search dog and its handler before they reached their designated area. He was reported to be cold and confused but was safely located and returned to safety. This incident highlights the importance of community and emergency services working together in search and rescue operations.

articles.title: Over 600 Homes Empty as Seven Sisters Evictions Continue in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: More than 600 homes are now vacant in Rochdale following the ongoing eviction of residents from the Seven Sisters tower blocks, with only 100 households remaining to be rehoused.
articles.content_html:
More than 600 homes now sit empty in Rochdale, nearly one year after the decision to evict the remaining 228 households from the Seven Sisters tower blocks, officially known as College Bank. As of late August 2026, only 100 households are left awaiting new accommodation out of approximately 760 total flats.

In October 2025, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) announced plans to empty all homes in the Seven Sisters due to safety concerns identified in a recent building survey. Issues highlighted included structural and electrical problems, water pumping system failures, roof damage, and rising costs for heating and lighting. Initially, residents were informed they might need to vacate by Christmas, but RBH later clarified that the evictions would occur over an 18-month period.

Since the announcement, 117 households have accepted offers for new homes, with 82 already relocated and 35 in the process of moving. Additionally, some residents have left through what RBH termed 'natural attrition', which includes reasons such as tenancy endings or voluntary departures. This leaves just over half of the original residents still needing rehousing.

The situation has been contentious, with local campaigners from the Save the Seven Sisters (ST7S) group expressing concerns over the potential demolition of the tower blocks. Although RBH has stated that no decision has been made regarding demolition, the uncertainty continues to affect residents. Mark Slater, chair of ST7S, has voiced strong opposition to the evictions, arguing that the safety issues cited by RBH are not immediate and calling the situation 'demolition by the back door'. RBH has committed to supporting all tenants during the relocation process, including financial assistance for those affected.

articles.title: Middleton Library Hosts 'How to Research Your House' Event for Heritage Open Days
articles.excerpt: Middleton Library invites residents to explore the history of their homes through a special event aimed at uncovering local heritage and notable past inhabitants.
articles.content_html:
Middleton Library and Local Studies Centre is inviting residents to participate in a special event titled 'How to Research Your House' as part of the Heritage Open Days initiative. The event aims to equip householders with the skills and tools necessary to delve into the history of their homes, including information about former inhabitants and changes to the local area.

Participants will learn how to uncover fascinating details about their properties, which may include connections to notable figures such as architect Edgar Wood and writer Samuel Bamford. The event also encourages attendees to explore whether their homes have links to local celebrities like actress Gracie Fields or actor Don Estelle, who lived in College Bank.

The borough of Rochdale features a diverse range of homes, from modern constructions to traditional properties, including former mills and settlements dating back to the 12th century, such as St Chad’s and the area around Broadfield Park. This event presents an opportunity for residents to bring the history of their properties to life, whether they are interested in celebrated residents or the more obscure, potentially spooky histories of their homes.

The 'How to Research Your House' event at Middleton Library is a valuable resource for those looking to connect with their local heritage. For more information about the event and how to participate, residents are encouraged to visit the Middleton Library website or contact the library directly.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The rocky cleft known locally as the Fairies’ Chapel is a well-loved part of Healey Dell’s landscape — a place of geology, industry and storytelling rather than documented supernatural events.
articles.summary: The rocky cleft known locally as the Fairies’ Chapel is a well-loved part of Healey Dell’s landscape — a place of geology, industry and storytelling rather than documented supernatural events.
articles.body:
Healey Dell’s Fairies’ Chapel is one of those local names that makes you slow your pace on the riverside path and look twice. The spot — a narrow gorge where the River Spodden squeezes through a cleft called the Thrutch — has been admired for centuries because the water-worn rock can take on shapes that, with a little imagination, suggest a pulpit, bench and alcove. The Dell itself is an established nature reserve and visitor attraction, with a heritage centre, tea rooms and family trails. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

The most concrete, documented facts are straightforward. Healey Dell is managed and promoted as a nature reserve by the borough and its industrial archaeology — mill sites, lodges and a striking Victorian railway viaduct — is part of the site’s real history. The viaduct that dominates the valley is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England (list entry 1317784). That history of mills and railways explains why the Dell became a popular Victorian beauty spot and why writers and guidebooks have long pointed to the peculiar rock features there. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

The “Fairies’ Chapel” name and the other colourful stories attached to the Thrutch come from the region’s rich oral and printed tradition. The best-known version of the tale appears in John Roby’s 19th‑century collection Traditions of Lancashire, where Roby records romances about a miller, a Lady Eleanor, an enchanted chapel, the Fairy Queen and prophecies tied to Healey. These are literary‑folklore accounts: vivid, localised retellings that collectors like Roby shaped for Victorian readers. They are valuable as records of what people told and believed, but they are not documentary proof that supernatural events occurred. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm))

Later local guides and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre reprise Roby’s material and other regional legends — including stories that mix fairies, witches and a fairy king — and they explain the physical origin of the name: erosive action by the river produced a cavernous niche that looked church‑like to observers. The centre also records local floods and landscape changes (for example an extreme storm on 4 July 1838 that altered sections of the Spodden valley), which helps explain why the rock features seen by earlier visitors are not exactly the same today. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

What can we say with reasonable certainty, and what is pure folklore? Facts: the place‑name and rock feature are real; Healey Dell’s industrial remains and railway viaduct are documented and protected; the site has been a site of local tourism since Victorian times. Legends: the tales of a Fairy King turning witches to stone, of prophetic fairy queens or of Robin Hood connections are elements of local storytelling preserved in collections like Roby’s and in later retellings — entertaining and culturally important, but unsupported by independent historical evidence. If a claim cannot be verified in archival records or contemporary sources, it should be treated as folklore. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

If you visit Healey Dell today, bring two pairs of eyes: one for the geology, mill ruins and the listed viaduct that really are there; the other for the stories people have told around that landscape for 150‑plus years. The Fairies’ Chapel is best enjoyed as a meeting place of nature, industrial history and imagination — a reminder that some places are important precisely because they gather stories as well as stones. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

articles.title: Why Rochdale says 'cruckle'
articles.excerpt: A short guide to a small but stubbornly local verb — what 'cruckle' means, where it comes from, and why dialect researchers care.
articles.summary: A short guide to a small but stubbornly local verb — what 'cruckle' means, where it comes from, and why dialect researchers care.
articles.body:
Anyone who grew up in parts of Rochdale will know the complaint: “I cruckled my ankle.” The word turns up in everyday speech to describe that awkward half‑twist you can walk off but which still makes you wince. That local usage — to roll or twist one’s ankle — is widely reported by speakers in and around the town and features in contemporary folk‑linguistic comments about Rochdale speech. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

But 'cruckle' is not a modern invention. Historical dialect sources show an older verb crookle (also spelled crookle/cruckle in some records) meaning “to bend, make crooked, stoop or hobble,” and this semantic field easily covers both bending and limping actions. The English Dialect Dictionary compiled by Joseph Wright (late 19th century) records crookle in northern and midland counties with senses that match those older meanings. ([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/englishdialectdi01wrig))

How did crookle become the very local‑sounding cruckle of Rochdale? Dialectists point to two processes common in northern English: (1) onomatopoeic and imitative formation around a crook/crook‑sound family (words that suggest bending or hooking), and (2) the frequentative suffix ‑le which forms verbs that describe repeated or small actions (so crook → crookle). Older comparative work on Germanic vocabulary links this group of words to related forms in other northern European dialects, which helps explain the form and range of meanings. In short, cruckle is a predictable local survival of an older dialect verb-group. ([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/englishdialectdi01wrig))

Is cruckle unique to Rochdale? Popular memory in the borough treats it as a Rochdale speciality, and recent perceptual and crowd‑sourced mapping of Greater Manchester dialects records respondents associating the term with Rochdale specifically (you can see it listed among the keywords used when people describe the borough’s speech). That evidence shows a strong local association today, even if identical or related forms occur elsewhere historically. In other words: Rochdale speakers claim and continue to use cruckle, and that social visibility makes it feel uniquely local. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

Where modern researchers and archivists come in: projects such as the British Library’s Word Bank and recent folk‑linguistic mapping work demonstrate how local words persist in everyday talk and are valuable evidence of small‑scale regional identity. Those projects flag items like cruckle because they show how vocabulary stays anchored to place even within a relatively small urban region. Linguists treat such items as data points for change, contact (for example, the Lancashire–Yorkshire boundary effects) and social meaning — words that signal where someone is from as much as how they walk. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/nov/24/british-library-project-discovers-two-new-words-thanks-to-guardian-readers))

What should readers take away? 'Cruckle' is a neat example of how a single verb preserves sound, meaning and local pride: rooted in older dialect forms recorded by nineteenth‑century lexicographers, visible today in crowdsourced dialect maps and oral memory, and meaningful because Rochdalians still use it. It is difficult to prove absolute exclusivity — dialect words rarely obey administrative borders — but both historical dictionaries and modern perceptual research make clear why people in Rochdale continue to say 'I cruckled' rather than 'I twisted' or 'I sprained.' If you have family uses or old spellings to share, local archives and dialect projects welcome contributions — these small words are exactly the material researchers need to trace how language and place stay entwined.
articles.content_html:
Anyone who grew up in parts of Rochdale will know the complaint: “I cruckled my ankle.” The word turns up in everyday speech to describe that awkward half‑twist you can walk off but which still makes you wince. That local usage — to roll or twist one’s ankle — is widely reported by speakers in and around the town and features in contemporary folk‑linguistic comments about Rochdale speech. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

But 'cruckle' is not a modern invention. Historical dialect sources show an older verb crookle (also spelled crookle/cruckle in some records) meaning “to bend, make crooked, stoop or hobble,” and this semantic field easily covers both bending and limping actions. The English Dialect Dictionary compiled by Joseph Wright (late 19th century) records crookle in northern and midland counties with senses that match those older meanings. ([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/englishdialectdi01wrig))

How did crookle become the very local‑sounding cruckle of Rochdale? Dialectists point to two processes common in northern English: (1) onomatopoeic and imitative formation around a crook/crook‑sound family (words that suggest bending or hooking), and (2) the frequentative suffix ‑le which forms verbs that describe repeated or small actions (so crook → crookle). Older comparative work on Germanic vocabulary links this group of words to related forms in other northern European dialects, which helps explain the form and range of meanings. In short, cruckle is a predictable local survival of an older dialect verb-group. ([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/englishdialectdi01wrig))

Is cruckle unique to Rochdale? Popular memory in the borough treats it as a Rochdale speciality, and recent perceptual and crowd‑sourced mapping of Greater Manchester dialects records respondents associating the term with Rochdale specifically (you can see it listed among the keywords used when people describe the borough’s speech). That evidence shows a strong local association today, even if identical or related forms occur elsewhere historically. In other words: Rochdale speakers claim and continue to use cruckle, and that social visibility makes it feel uniquely local. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

Where modern researchers and archivists come in: projects such as the British Library’s Word Bank and recent folk‑linguistic mapping work demonstrate how local words persist in everyday talk and are valuable evidence of small‑scale regional identity. Those projects flag items like cruckle because they show how vocabulary stays anchored to place even within a relatively small urban region. Linguists treat such items as data points for change, contact (for example, the Lancashire–Yorkshire boundary effects) and social meaning — words that signal where someone is from as much as how they walk. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/nov/24/british-library-project-discovers-two-new-words-thanks-to-guardian-readers))

What should readers take away? 'Cruckle' is a neat example of how a single verb preserves sound, meaning and local pride: rooted in older dialect forms recorded by nineteenth‑century lexicographers, visible today in crowdsourced dialect maps and oral memory, and meaningful because Rochdalians still use it. It is difficult to prove absolute exclusivity — dialect words rarely obey administrative borders — but both historical dictionaries and modern perceptual research make clear why people in Rochdale continue to say 'I cruckled' rather than 'I twisted' or 'I sprained.' If you have family uses or old spellings to share, local archives and dialect projects welcome contributions — these small words are exactly the material researchers need to trace how language and place stay entwined.

articles.title: Boy, 13, stabbed in Rochdale town centre: six arrested, two bailed and stop-and-search powers extended
articles.excerpt: Live story. Six teenage boys have now been arrested after a 13-year-old was stabbed in Rochdale town centre on Saturday night. Two have been released on bail, four remain in custody, and Section 60 stop-and-search powers in the town centre run until 3pm on Tuesday. Updated as Greater Manchester Police confirm developments.
articles.content_html:
Latest, 08:30, Tuesday 1 September: six teenage boys have been arrested in connection with the stabbing of a 13-year-old boy in Rochdale town centre on Saturday night, 29 August. Two were arrested on Sunday and have since been released on bail. Four more were arrested on Monday and remain in custody. All six were held on suspicion of assault and possession of a bladed article, Greater Manchester Police said. The injured boy remains in hospital receiving treatment.

This is Rochdale Daily's single live story on the incident. It is updated in place, newest first, only when Greater Manchester Police or another primary source confirms a development. Earlier separate reports have been folded into this page; see the correction note at the foot.

What we know

The boy was stabbed during a serious assault in the town centre, near the Riverside shopping centre, on the evening of Saturday 29 August. Police described the incident as a serious assault alongside wider disorder in the town centre that night. He was taken to hospital, where he remains.

Monday 31 August: GMP confirmed four further arrests, all teenage boys, on suspicion of assault and possession of a bladed article. The two boys arrested on Sunday were released on bail while enquiries continue. Detective Superintendent Richard Hunt said the force was continuing to make progress on the investigation and that violence on the streets would not be tolerated.

Monday 31 August: the Section 60 order covering Rochdale town centre was extended until 3pm on Tuesday 1 September. Under Section 60 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act, officers can stop and search people in the designated area without needing reasonable suspicion.

Sunday 30 August: GMP announced two arrests and put a 24-hour Section 60 order in place for the town centre from 3pm. Chief Inspector Michael Barton, neighbourhoods lead for GMP's Rochdale district, said detectives were reviewing CCTV, gathering witness statements and analysing intelligence to identify everyone involved.

Saturday 29 August: a 13-year-old boy was stabbed in the town centre. GMP log 2750 of 29/08/2026.

What we do not know

Police have not released the boy's condition beyond confirming he remains in hospital, and have not said what led to the assault. No one has been charged. Rochdale Daily will not name anyone arrested and will not publish speculation about motive or identity while the investigation is live.

How to help the investigation

Anyone who witnessed the incident, was in Rochdale town centre on Saturday evening, or has mobile phone, CCTV or dashcam footage is asked to contact GMP on 101, quoting log 2750 of 29/08/2026, or via the LiveChat function at gmp.police.uk. Information can be given anonymously to Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

Story first published 30 August 2026 as "Two arrested following stabbing incident in Rochdale"; consolidated into this live page on 1 September 2026.

All those arrested are under investigation and have not been charged. Nothing in this report should be taken as an indication of guilt. It will be updated as verified information becomes available.

articles.title: Rochdale AFC Secures 3-0 Victory Against Shrewsbury Town
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Football Club achieved a significant 3-0 victory over Shrewsbury Town, marking their first win since returning to the EFL. Manager Ian Watson praised the team's performance for its courage and bravery.
articles.content_html:
ONGOING STORY — Updated 1 September 2026 at 08:28. 62 source updates have been combined into this article.

Rochdale AFC celebrated their first win of the season with a convincing 3-0 victory against Shrewsbury Town at the Crown Oil Arena on Tuesday evening, 1st September 2026. This win marks a significant turnaround for the team, who have recently returned to the English Football League (EFL).

The match saw Rochdale take control early on, with Kane Taylor's cross nearly resulting in a goal when Dajaune Brown's header skimmed the crossbar. The home side broke the deadlock in the 33rd minute when Baba Adeeko capitalised on a rebound to score with a right-footed effort past Shrewsbury's goalkeeper, Will Brook.

Rochdale extended their lead just before half-time, with Luke Hannant scoring after intercepting a pass and finishing expertly from 18 yards. The second half saw further chances for Rochdale, including a notable save from Shrewsbury's goalkeeper to deny Will Boyle's header.

The scoring was rounded off in the 80th minute by substitute Jonny Smith, who curled a shot into the net after a swift run down the right flank. This victory not only boosts Rochdale's morale but also lifts them off the bottom of League Two, providing a much-needed confidence boost as they look to build on this success in upcoming matches.

Update timeline

  • 1 September 2026, 08:28: Rochdale AFC Secures 3-0 Victory Against Shrewsbury Town
  • 31 August 2026, 14:03: Rochdale AFC Secures 3-0 Victory Against Shrewsbury Town
